rewrite.question: What does `child_process.spawn(cmd, args)` return with the default stdio settings?

rewrite.question: Which statement describes a cryptographic hash function?
rewrite.hint: Ask two things about the same input hashed twice: do you get the same digest, and can anyone turn the digest back into the input?
rewrite.explanation: A cryptographic hash maps any input to a fixed-size digest that is deterministic (the same input always gives the same digest) and one-way: there is no key and no inverse operation, so the input cannot be recovered from the digest. rewrite.hint: Recall how the captured value is read back (req.params.id) and which path character Express uses to mark a segment as a named capture.
rewrite.explanation: Express marks a named parameter with a colon: '/users/:id' matches /users/42 and puts '42' in req.params.id. The other spellings come from elsewhere. {id} is OpenAPI/Spring style; in Express 5 braces mean an optional literal segment, so '/users/{id}' matches /users/ and /users/id and captures nothing. [id] is Next.js file routing and Express 5 rejects it as an unescaped reserved character, and a bare * wildcard must now be named, as in '/files/*splat'.

rationale: Key verified; the distractors are genuinely borrowed from other systems, which is good. The explanation should say what each does in Express 5, all of which was checked at runtime.

objective: Explain Node's I/O concurrency model: one JavaScript thread driving a non-blocking event loop rather than a thread per request.
defects: hint is the generic fallback

options: It starts one operating-system thread per incoming request
It runs JavaScript on one thread and lets a non-blocking event loop overlap I/O
It polls every open socket in a tight loop until data arrives

rewrite.hint: Ask what a Node process is doing while a database query is in flight: waiting on that query, or free to handle other events.
rewrite.explanation: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread and asks the operating system for non-blocking I/O; the event loop (libuv, using epoll, kqueue or IOCP) waits on many sockets at once and runs each callback when its data arrives, so thousands of connections overlap without a thread each. Thread-per-request is how classic servers such as Apache prefork work, busy-polling would burn the CPU, and callbacks never get their own threads; only some file-system and crypto calls use a small libuv thread pool behind the scenes.

rationale: The keyed model is correct and foundational for the Concurrency level. Two distractors are filler and the explanation should name the OS mechanism and the thread-pool exception.

rewrite.hint: Ask which thread the timer and I/O callbacks need in order to run, and who is holding it during the calculation.
rewrite.explanation: Node runs all JavaScript, including every timer and I/O callback, on one thread. While the image calculation occupies it the event loop cannot advance, so unrelated callbacks queue until the calculation returns and every client of that process waits. Callbacks never get their own thread and Node never moves code to worker threads on its own; you have to offload with worker_threads or a child process, or split the work into smaller chunks.

rewrite.hint: Contrast it with child_process.fork and ask what the word 'thread' changes about isolation and memory.
rewrite.explanation: worker_threads starts additional V8 threads inside the same Node process; each worker runs its own JavaScript with its own event loop, communicates through postMessage, and can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. That makes it the tool for CPU-heavy work such as parsing or image processing. child_process and cluster start separate processes with IPC, a single thread can never run two callbacks at once, and network I/O is already non-blocking on the event loop, so workers add nothing there.

rationale: Key verified by running a Worker (same pid, different thread id). The item needs distractors that test the process/thread distinction instead of nonsense, plus a specific hint.
evidence: node: new Worker(..., {eval:true}) reported isMainThread false, threadId 1 and the same process.pid as the main thread; its Atomics writes were visible in the main thread's SharedArrayBuffer

https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/worker_threads.html: 'Workers (threads) are useful for performing CPU-intensive JavaScript operations. They do not help much with I/O-intensive work.' and 'Unlike child_process or cluster, worker_threads can share memory.'

objective: Identify which asynchronous Node APIs run on libuv's worker pool (fs, some crypto, dns.lookup, zlib) as opposed to the event loop's non-blocking polling, timers and microtasks.
defects: hint is the generic fallback

rewrite.hint: Ask which of these operations the operating system cannot deliver as a non-blocking event, so libuv has to run a blocking call on a background thread instead.
rewrite.explanation: fs.readFile and crypto.pbkdf2 both run on libuv's worker pool: most operating systems have no non-blocking file API, and pbkdf2 is CPU-bound, so libuv executes them on one of its four default threads (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE) and posts the result back. dns.lookup and asynchronous zlib calls use the pool as well. Timers, microtasks and queueMicrotask are event-loop bookkeeping, socket reads use the OS's non-blocking polling, and JSON.parse or a loop simply run on the main thread.

rationale: A well-built item: the pairs are clean, the key matches the Node CLI and event-loop docs, and the pool effect was measured. Only the hint is filler; the explanation gains the 'why' and the pool size.
evidence: https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/cli.html UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE: 'Node.js APIs that use the threadpool are: all fs APIs, other than the file watcher APIs and those that are explicitly synchronous; asynchronous crypto APIs such as crypto.pbkdf2(), crypto.scrypt(), crypto.randomBytes(), crypto.randomFill(), crypto.generateKeyPair(); dns.lookup(); all zlib APIs, other than those that are explicitly synchronous'
node: 4 concurrent crypto.pbkdf2 calls on a 4-CPU machine took 404 ms with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 and 109 ms with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4
https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop: network I/O is fulfilled by the event loop (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), not the Worker Pool
